sharedText: this is the thing that ye shall do
reason: A five-word run and the only candidate the machine offers at this verse. Judges 21:11 is the order to slaughter Jabesh-gilead — “Ye shall utterly destroy every male, and every woman that hath lain by man” — and 3 Nephi 27:7 is “whatsoever ye shall do, ye shall do it in my name”. The overlap is the bare English of instruction, “ye shall do”, doubled in each verse by accident of construction: the Book of Mormon doubles it because it is building an anaphora on “in my name”, Judges because it is glossing a vow. No content word is shared. Covered in principle by the standing exclusion for connective boilerplate, and written out because the ranking is high enough that a reader working from the dossier would meet it.

Hardy cross-references Matthew 16:18 at this verse, and the association is sound at the level a study edition works at: 27:8 is the founding statement about what makes a church Christ's, and Matthew 16:18 is the KJV's one verse in which Christ says “I will build my church”. But the verbal contact here is two words, “my church”, in a verse whose argument is about naming rather than building — “how be it my church, save it be called in my name?” — and “upon this rock I will build my church” is already adjudicated in this book at 3 Nephi 11:39, where the Book of Mormon has the rock, the building and the gates-of-hell clause together. Putting the link where the wording is (CONVENTIONS §6a) sends it to 11:39; a reader at 27:8 is sent there from here. What 27:8 does add to 11:39 is the naming argument, which has no Matthew 16 warrant at all: Matthew 16:18 never says the church is called anything.

Hardy also cross-references Matthew 7:24-27 here, the wise and foolish builders, and the pull is real because 27:8-11 turns entirely on what a church is “built upon” — the gospel, or the works of men, or the works of the devil. The wording will not carry it. Matthew 7:24-27's distinctive vocabulary is the rock, the sand, the rain, the floods, the winds, the house and the great fall, and 3 Nephi 27:8-11 has none of the seven; what it shares is the participle “built upon”, which is ordinary English. The parable itself is adjudicated in this book twice already, at 3 Nephi 14:24-27 where it is transcribed whole and at 3 Nephi 11:40 and 18:13 where its closing verses are applied. The Matthew 7 contact that this chapter really does make is elsewhere: 27:11's “hewn down and cast into the fire” from 7:19, and 27:29 and 27:33 from 7:7-8 and 7:13-14, all of which are linked.

The top-ranked candidate at this verse on a five-word run, and it is the wrong half of the sentence. What 1 Timothy 1:15 contributes is “Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners”, and “came into the world” is a formula the KJV uses of Christ at John 1:9, 6:14, 11:27, 12:46, 16:28, 18:37 and 1 Timothy 1:15 — too widely spread to identify a source, and used in the Book of Mormon constantly. The purpose clause is where the borrowing is, and it is Johannine, not Pauline: “to do the will of my Father, because my Father sent me” answers to John 6:38 and John 4:34, which are linked at this verse. 1 Timothy's purpose clause, saving sinners, is not in 3 Nephi 27:13 at all.

sharedText: what ye have seen me do
reason: The register's best entry in this chapter, because the run is genuinely long — “ye have seen me do”, five words — and because a reader who finds it will assume the catalogue missed it. Judges 9:48 is Abimelech on mount Zalmon: he cuts a bough from a tree, lays it on his shoulder, and tells his men “What ye have seen me do, make haste, and do as I have done” — whereupon they each cut a bough, pile them against the tower of Shechem and burn about a thousand men and women alive inside it. 3 Nephi 27:21 is “the works which ye have seen me do, that shall ye also do”, spoken to the twelve about their ministry. The clause is identical and every term of the situation is inverted: the model is a usurper, the imitation is an atrocity, and the point of the sentence in Judges is speed rather than fidelity. The real source of the construction is John 14:12, the only KJV verse with “the works that I do shall he do also”, which is linked here; Judges 9:48 is what an n-gram window returns when a very ordinary English clause happens to have been used once by Abimelech.

A five-word run, and both verses attach a promise to a conditional — 2 Peter 1:10 “if ye do these things, ye shall never fall”, 3 Nephi 27:22 “if ye do these things, blessed are ye, for ye shall be lifted up at the last day”. The shared string is the conditional itself and nothing else: 2 Peter's “these things” are the virtues of the ladder in 1:5-7, the Book of Mormon's are the works of 27:21, and the apodoses share no word. “If ye do these things” is not a KJV singleton in any useful sense; it is how English joins a condition to a consequence. Note that the genuine 2 Peter contact in this chapter is at 27:27, where “what manner of persons ought ye to be” is a singleton at 2 Peter 3:11 and is linked.

A five-word run made entirely of an interjection and a quantifier. Luke 11:41 ends the woe about the outside of the cup — “give alms of such things as ye have; and, behold, all things are clean unto you” — and 3 Nephi 27:26 is “behold, all things are written by the Father”. The predicate, which is the only part that carries meaning, is different in each. Filed rather than passed over in silence because the run ranks in the chapter's top twenty-four and because a reader might expect the catalogue to have considered the cup-and-platter material given how much of Matthew 23 and Luke 11 the Book of Mormon uses elsewhere; it does not use it here.

sharedText: for silver, and for gold, and for
reason: A seven-word run and the highest-ranked machine candidate at this verse, and it is a list. 2 Chronicles 32:27 inventories Hezekiah's treasuries — “for silver, and for gold, and for precious stones, and for spices, and for shields” — and 3 Nephi 27:32 is “they will sell me for silver, and for gold, and for that which moth doth corrupt”. The run is produced by the KJV's way of coordinating a series with a repeated preposition, and it survives seven words only because both series happen to begin with the same two metals, which is the order the KJV always uses. Nothing of Hezekiah is here. The verse's real sources are Matthew 6:19, whose “thieves break through and steal” is a singleton and which supplies the third member of the Book of Mormon's list, and John 17:12; both are linked. The betrayal price behind “sell me for silver” is Matthew 26:15's thirty pieces, recorded there as a composite rather than as a separate row, since the Book of Mormon has neither the number nor the KJV's verb.
